nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
Continuing along the lines of #56385, Transformers are a very popular model and we should be working to make sure that we optimize them.
A common pattern in transformers is to apply query, key, and value linear layers on the same input, where all three linear layers have the same size weights.
If you check out the Using TorchScript in Python section here
And then modify the final two lines to print:
traced_model = torch.jit.trace(model, [tokens_tensor, segments_tensors])
frozen_model = torch.jit.freeze(traced_model.eval())
print(frozen_model.graph)

You should see a number of these patterns:
  %input.29 : Tensor = aten::layer_norm(%input.27, %1478, %self.encoder.layer.0.output.LayerNorm.weight, %self.encoder.layer.0.output.LayerNorm.bias, %50, %51)
  %x.13 : Tensor = aten::linear(%input.29, %self.encoder.layer.1.attention.self.query.weight, %self.encoder.layer.1.attention.self.query.bias)
  %x.17 : Tensor = aten::linear(%input.29, %self.encoder.layer.1.attention.self.key.weight, %self.encoder.layer.1.attention.self.key.bias)
  %x.21 : Tensor = aten::linear(%input.29, %self.encoder.layer.1.attention.self.value.weight, %self.encoder.layer.1.attention.self.value.bias)

We can optimize this pattern by concatenating all of the respective weights/biases, and then chunk the output into three different tensors.
The following micro-benchmark shows the speedup of this optimization for the input/weight sizes found in this link, and the matmul sizes mentioned for BERT by this paper.
import torch
import time
from itertools import product

inp_sizes = [
    ((1, 14, 768), (768, 768), (768,)),
    ((64, 1024), (4096, 1024), (4096,)),    
]


for device, sizes in product(["cpu", "cuda"], inp_sizes):
    inp = torch.rand(sizes[0]).to(device)
    weights = [torch.rand(sizes[1]).to(device) for _ in range(3)]
    biases = [torch.rand(sizes[2]).to(device) for _ in range(3)]
    
    warmup = 5
    outputs = [0 for _ in range(3)]
    def test():
        for i in range(3):
            outputs[i] = torch._C._nn.linear(inp, weights[i], biases[i])
    
    NITER = 15
    NWARMUP = 3

    def benchmark(func):
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        for _ in range(NWARMUP):
            func()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        s = time.time()
        for _ in range(NITER):
            func()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
        e = time.time()
        return (e - s) / NITER
    
    non_fused = benchmark(test)    
    weights = torch.cat(weights)
    biases = torch.cat(biases)
    outputs2 = []
    
    def fused():
        out = torch._C._nn.linear(inp, weights, biases)
        outputs2 = torch.chunk(out, 3)
        
    fused = benchmark(fused)
    for elem1, elem2 in zip(outputs, outputs2):
        torch.testing.assert_allclose(elem1, elem2)
        
    print("sizes", sizes, "device", device, "fused speedup", (non_fused - fused)/non_fused)


sizes ((1, 14, 768), (768, 768), (768,)) device cpu fused speedup 0.29792242952151143
sizes ((64, 1024), (4096, 1024), (4096,)) device cpu fused speedup -0.041824412288446286
sizes ((1, 14, 768), (768, 768), (768,)) device cuda fused speedup 0.47636900704385365
sizes ((64, 1024), (4096, 1024), (4096,)) device cuda fused speedup 0.34117876531972297

As you can see, this optimization provides a very nice speedup on GPU, while being less clear for CPU. In this first version of the issue we will only implement it for GPU.
We are going to want to add it as part of the frozen optimization pipeline.
Potentially helpful links: frozen optimizations, code inspecting constant tensor inputs.
In the future we could consider extending thiss type of concatenation and chunking pattern to other operators, and do light-weight autotuning to determine if it is profitable to do this on CPU (additionally, we would need to update our MKLDNN fusion pass to handle chunk if we add it to CPU).

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
A common idiom in PyTorch is to have an optional inplace parameter as an input to activation modules. An example of this is here in the pytorch benchmark repro.
When you script this module, the if inplace logic prevents fusing the activation with adjacent pointwise ops. A solution here is to rewrite mutation on activations, so that both branches are the same.
  %7 : bool = prim::GetAttr[name="inplace"](%self)
  %result : Tensor = prim::If(%7)
    block0():
      %result.1 : Tensor = aten::relu6_(%6)
      -> (%result.1)
    block1():
      %result.3 : Tensor = aten::relu6(%6)
      -> (%result.3)

->
  %7 : bool = prim::GetAttr[name="inplace"](%self)
  %result : Tensor = prim::If(%7)
    block0():
      %result.1 : Tensor = aten::relu6(%6)
      -> (%result.1)
    block1():
      %result.3 : Tensor = aten::relu6(%6)
      -> (%result.3)

At which point we can move the relu6 computation above the if node.
->
  %7 : bool = prim::GetAttr[name="inplace"](%self)
  %result.1 : Tensor = aten::relu6(%6)
  %result : Tensor = prim::If(%7)
    block0():
      -> (%result.1)
    block1():
      -> (%result.1)

This issue would start with the graph with mutation removed and two relu6 nodes and produce the final graph. We do not need to go too crazy with making the pass overly general or covering many cases since we have a targeted use case here, and don't expect much gain from additional logic.
A relevant pass to look at is our Common Subexpression Elimination Pass.
Note: right now the RemoveMutation pass doesn't remove the mutation on relu6_, that could be a good follow up or related task for this to actually fire.
cc @gmagogsfm

🚀 Feature
Follow up from #47112
A NumPy-like from_buffer function for creating a tensor without copying data.
Alternatives
Apparently, people were using Storage.from_buffer and passing it to the constructor instead. There are two problems with it, though:

When the legacy constructor is deprecated, so will be the means to create a tensor from a Storage object.
As far as I can tell, Storage.from_buffer does copy the data.

Code in torchvision:
img = torch.ByteTensor(torch.ByteStorage.from_buffer(pic.tobytes()))
That said, it's possible to do it through NumPy, by using the torch.from_numpy function.

The goal of this tasks is to provide a convenient hook system for SavedVariables.
The hooks will be a pair of python functions:

One that goes from the current Tensor to any python object
A second that will be able to transform that python back into the original Tensor

These operations don't need to be differentiable and any gradient information on the returned Tensor will be overwritten to have proper history.

Write a generic c++ class and a python-specialized implementation to hold the hooks (similar to anomaly_mode.h/python_anomaly_mode.h)
Write a python binding to be able to access the SavedVariable (via pybind like c10::InferenceMode) to be able to add such hook
Update the SavedVariable to apply such hook (pre-processing when the hook is added and post-processing while unpacking)

Autograd property save needs to happen during pre-processing
The rewrapping of the returned Tensor should be very similar to the current unpack function
The user hooks should run in no-grad mode
Inplace tests don't need to happen

Not sure if this is a bug or expected behavior, but opening the issue for discussion/clarification. In the following repro, b is not used for loss computation and therefore I'd expect the gradient for the linear layer self.b to stay as None, however, the gradient is 0:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Function


class PassThrough(Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, *inputs):
        return inputs

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, *grad_outputs):
        print(f"grad_outputs {grad_outputs}")
        return grad_outputs


class MyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.a = nn.Linear(1, 1, bias=False)
        self.b = nn.Linear(1, 1, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        a, b = self.a(x), self.b(x)
        ret = a, b
        new_a, new_b = PassThrough.apply(a, b)
        ret = new_a, new_b
        return ret

model = MyModel()

def print_grads():
    for param_name, param in model.named_parameters():
        print(f"{param_name} : {param.grad}")


inp = torch.ones(1)
print("-- before backward ---")
model.zero_grad()
print_grads()

model.zero_grad()
out = model(inp)
loss = out[0].sum()
print("Calling backward...")
loss.backward()
print("-- after bwd --")
print_grads()

This produces the output:
-- before backward ---
a.weight : None
b.weight : None
Calling backward...
grad_outputs (tensor([1.]), tensor([0.]))
-- after bwd --
a.weight : tensor([[1.]])
b.weight : tensor([[0.]])

It looks like since out[1] is not used in computing loss, the torch.autograd.Function fills in a 0 for the corresponding grad tensor in grad_outputs, and as a result, the .grad field gets set to 0.  However, this particular torch.autograd.Function as defined doesn't really do anything (it just forwards the inputs/outputs) so I would expect it the resulting gradients to not be different than if the torch.autograd.Function was not used. When the torch.autograd.Function usage is omitted from the forward pass, the gradient for b is not touched as expected:
-- before backward ---
a.weight : None
b.weight : None
Calling backward...
-- after bwd --
a.weight : tensor([[1.]])
b.weight : None

Ideally I would expect it to be the same even with the torch.autograd.Function, since the gradients are not modified at all. Would appreciate any comments/thoughts on this, thank you!

nodes.bodyText:
When using custom autograd.Function, it is easy to save an intermediary result in the context like ctx.foo and then use it during the backward pass.
Unfortunately, if that value is actually linked to the input/output gradient computation, the double backward computation will be wrong because the contribution of ctx.foo will be ignored.
We can reduce this risk by intercepting all Tensors that are saved onto ctx. during the forward pass and attaching to them a grad_fn that will fail during the double backward pass if this Tensor was used during that computation in a differentiable manner.
The error should suggest to the user to make such intermediary result an output of the function so that it will have a proper grad_fn associated with it.
A bad example is:
import torch
from torch import autograd

class BadCustomFunction(autograd.Function):
  @staticmethod
  def forward(ctx, inp):
    interm = inp * 2
    ctx.foo = interm
    res = interm ** 2
    return res

  @staticmethod
  def backward(ctx, gres):
      grad = 2 * 2 * ctx.foo * gres
      return grad


inp = torch.rand(2, dtype=torch.double, requires_grad=True)
# Gradcheck is correct
autograd.gradcheck(BadCustomFunction.apply, inp)  # True
# Double grad is silently wrong
autograd.gradgradcheck(BadCustomFunction.apply, inp)  # False
cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @soulitzer @lezcano
nodes.title: custom Function intermediary results are dangerous for double backward

        return x


def run_toy(net, batch_dim, train, use_mkldnn, iter_cnt=100, batch_size=2):
    start_time = time.time()

    if train:
        net.train()
    else:
        net.eval()

    if use_mkldnn:
        net = mkldnn_utils.to_mkldnn(net)

    for i in range(iter_cnt):  # fake batch iteration
        batch = torch.rand(batch_size, batch_dim)  # fake batch
        if use_mkldnn:
            batch = batch.to_mkldnn()

        if train:
            output_batch = net(batch)

            loss_func = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
            loss = loss_func(output_batch, torch.randn(batch_size, 1))
            loss.sum().backward()

        else:
            with torch.no_grad():
                output_batch = net(batch)

    print(f'Time: {time.time() - start_time}s')

nodes.bodyText:
SavedVariable is current doing unwrapping as:

For leaf, save a weak pointer to its grad-accumulator
If the Tensor is an output of the function, save a weak pointer to its grad_fn
If the Tensor is none of the above, save a strong pointer to its grad_fn

On top of that, it also unpacks the version counter, forward gradients, requires grad field and a .data of the Tensor itself.
This allows the SavedVariable to reconstruct a similar Tensor when it is requested during the backward.
The first and third categories here though don't actually need to go through the whole unwrapping and the given Tensor can be kept as-is (the saved version and data reset logic will need to remain of course).
This task would consist in updating this logic to keep the original Tensor as is in these cases and add corresponding tests.

I have once reported the speed problem of RTX 3090 in #54408
Thanks for everyone who gave me advices and reported the similar problem.
I am using the function which converts euler angles to rotation matrix (similar to link).
I compared the computation results from the following settings:

RTX 3090 + PyTorch 1.8.1 with CUDA 11.1
GTX 1080 Ti + PyTorch 1.8.1 with CUDA 10.2
PyTorch 1.8.1 (CPU mode)
NumPy

The results from the last 3 were the same, whereas that from RTX 3090 were totally different.
I think I should also try 'GTX 1080 Ti + PyTorch 1.8.1 with CUDA 11.1', but I am sorry I have not.

🚀 Feature
TensorPipe uses some advanced features of the Linux kernel. It does so on a "best effort" basis (i.e., use them if available, fall back on something else if not). This logic is unfortunately hard to test because it would require specific kernel versions on our CI machines. So it occasionally happens that we find out about issues when users report them. To help investigate these reports we've found it useful to know the kernel version and the glibc version used by the user (both when building and when running, if they're different). It would be great if these could be added to the report produced by collect_env.

nodes.bodyText:
The current implementation of torch.testing.assert_close already does a good job at delivering information to the user in case of mismatching values. Still, I think they can be improved in multiple ways:


If a scalar (tensor) is compared, the error message currently looks like this:
AssertionError: Tensors are not close!

Mismatched elements: 1 / 1 (100.0%)
Greatest absolute difference: 1.0 at 0 (up to 1e-05 allowed)
Greatest relative difference: 0.5 at 0 (up to 1.3e-06 allowed)

This can be improved in multiple ways:

The header should read "Scalars are not close!" to indicate that only a single value was involved in the comparison
The number of mismatched elements should be removed since it carries no information and always is Mismatched elements: 1 / 1 (100.0%)
The word "Greatest" should be removed from the reported absolute and relative differences, since there is only one difference each
The index should be removed since it carries no information and scalar tensors cannot accessed by index

With these changes the error message could look like:
AssertionError: Scalars are not close!

Absolute difference: 1.0 at 0 (up to 1e-05 allowed)
Relative difference: 0.5 at 0 (up to 1.3e-06 allowed)



The only differences between the messages for closeness and equality are that

the header reads "not close"  instead of "not equal" and
the allowed tolerances are appended to the differences.

We could combine the two by making the message dependent on the value of the tolerances:

The header should read "equal" if rtol == 0 and atol == 0 and
the allowed tolerance should only be added if > 0

This would also allow us to make assert_equal a special case of assert_close (#56544 (comment)) without further modification.


By default the numbers in the error message are formatted with the "General format" (:g). This might lead to diverging formats of two related numbers if they have different magnitudes:
abs_diff = 1e-4
atol = 1e-5
print(f"Absolute difference: {abs_diff} (up to {atol} allowed)")
Absolute difference: 0.0001 (up to 1e-05 allowed)

We should use a fixed number format, e.g, :.2e for floats and :d for integers.


Non-matching NaN's currently eliminate the difference information in the error message:
a = torch.tensor(1.0, float("NaN"))
b = torch.tensor(2.0, float("NaN"))
torch.testing.assert_close(a, b)

AssertionError: Tensors are not close!
Mismatched elements: 2 / 2 (100.0%)
Greatest absolute difference: nan at 1 (up to 1e-05 allowed)
Greatest relative difference: nan at 1 (up to 1.3e-06 allowed)

We should exclude NaN's from the difference calculation and for example add a line Mismatched NaN's: ... in case there are any.


assert_close allows to pass a callable as msg to construct an expressive error message. If a user just wants to add some information, for example the tested operator, it is currently impossible to do without losing all the benefits of our message generation. We should make our version public so others can build on top of it:
import torch.testing

def my_msg(actual, expected, info):
    default_msg = torch.testing.default_mismatch_msg(actual, expected, info)
    return f"My important information: ... \n\n{default_msg}"

torch.testing.assert_close(..., msg=my_msg)
nodes.title: Improve error messages of `torch.testing.assert_close` in case of mismatching values

🐛 Bug
When an object of tensor's subclass is saved in torch.autograd.Function using ctx.save_for_backward, the type is not preserved in the backward method when accessing it with ctx.saved_tensors.
To Reproduce
This is an example script to illustrate what I meant:
import torch

class SubTensor(torch.Tensor):
    pass

a = SubTensor([2]).requires_grad_()
b = torch.tensor(1.0).requires_grad_()

class Fcn(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, a, b):
        ctx.save_for_backward(a, b)
        print("a in forward :", type(a))
        c = a * b
        return c
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_c):
        a, b = ctx.saved_tensors
        print("a in backward:", type(a))
        return b * grad_c, a * grad_c

c = Fcn.apply(a, b)
print("c            :", type(c))
da, db = torch.autograd.grad(c, (a, b))
print("da           :", type(da))
print("db           :", type(db))

The script above prints:
a in forward : <class '__main__.SubTensor'>
c            : <class '__main__.SubTensor'>
a in backward: <class 'torch.Tensor'>
da           : <class '__main__.SubTensor'>
db           : <class '__main__.SubTensor'>

When saved in forward method, the type of a is SubTensor. However, when accessed in backward, the type of a is torch.Tensor.
Expected behavior
I'm not sure if this is what PyTorch's team expected, but I expect that the type of a should be preserved in the backward method.
Environment

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
Slicing moduleList fails with given stepped size gives an error.
To Reproduce
class Foo(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        m1 = torch.nn.Linear(1,2)
        m2 = torch.nn.ReLU()
        self.test = torch.nn.ModuleList([m1,m2])
    def forward(self):
        return self.test[::-1][0], self.test[::-1][1]

f = Foo()
self.checkModule(Foo(), ())

gives following error:
AssertionError: ReLU() != <torch._C.ScriptModule object at 0x7f8c36f64030>

This is because slicing moduleList silently ignores the step size.
Expected behavior
Shouldn't fail
Additional context
This is because we refactored the original tuple slicing logic but never touched the part where we convert moduleList to tuple to slice it.
cc @gmagogsfm

🐛 Bug
If a Tensor backward hook removes itself during execution and returns a modified gradient, PyTorch will segfault.
To Reproduce
import torch

def install_hook(tensor):
    handle = None
    def hook(tensor):
        handle.remove()
        return torch.zeros_like(tensor)
    handle = tensor.register_hook(hook)

def test_hook():
    t = torch.ones((1, 5))
    t.requires_grad_()
    install_hook(t)
    (t ** 2).mean().backward()
    print(t.grad)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    test_hook()

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug

Docs mention that bias is initialized as UninitializedParameter but all the lazy modules have bias as a Parameter.
# To Reproduce
import torch

print(list(torch.nn.LazyLinear(10, 5).named_parameters()))

"""
[('weight', Uninitialized parameter), ('bias', Parameter containing:
tensor([ 0.0000e+00, -2.5244e-29, -9.3202e+27, -2.0005e+00,  1.1210e-44,
         0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00],
       requires_grad=True))]
"""

print(list(torch.nn.LazyConv2d(10, 5, 5).named_parameters()))

"""
[('weight', Uninitialized parameter), ('bias', Parameter containing:
tensor([ 0.0000e+00, -2.5244e-29, -9.3202e+27, -2.0005e+00,  1.1210e-44,
        -0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  3.5873e-43,  3.6013e-43],
       requires_grad=True))]
"""
Expected behavior
Either bias should be an Uninitialized parameter or the docs should mention that bias is initialized before the weights.

nodes.title: topk triggers device assert

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
HardSwish ONNX export has been added in #48423, but it is exported as a series of primitive ops (Add, Clip, Div). ONNX already has the HardSigmoid op since opset 6 and will have a dedicated HardSwish op since opset 14. For now, we can change it to export as x * HardSigmoid(x) for simplicity.
In fact, nn.HardSigmoid() op has already been exported as HardSigmoid op directly in #54193. Please use this as a reference for fixing HardSwish.
On the practical side, when exporting MobileNetV3 to ONNX, currently all the HardSwish activations are exported as primitives, which makes the graph very big.

Expected behavior
Change to export nn.HardSwish() as x * HardSigmoid(x) directly instead of primitive ops to reduce ONNX graph size.

cc @houseroad @spandantiwari @lara-hdr @BowenBao @neginraoof @SplitInfinity
nodes.title: HardSwish ONNX export is not optimized.

nodes.bodyText:
Updated 6/7/2021
PyTorch once had "tensor_op_tests", but they were removed in #55558. These tests would run a method once on the CPU and once on a CUDA or XLA device and compare the results. What these tests did and how they should be used was confusing, however, and they were often added when it was unnecessary to do so or removed as OpInfos were created for them, even though the OpInfo tests do not yet cover the same cases.
After some discussion (see below), instead of using the CPU as the source of truth, we would like to generalize the OpInfo architecture to support references. UnaryUfuncInfos already support references, but the OpInfo base class does not. This reference can then be compared against PyTorch's implementation of the operation on its sample inputs.
cc @mruberry @VitalyFedyunin @walterddr @kshitij12345 @krshrimali -- maybe an interesting task for @krshrimali's onboarding?
nodes.title: Create an OpInfo test for CPU vs CUDA consistency

nodes.bodyText:
This RFC is inspired by @eellison's suggestions for improving OpInfo usability here: #57577.
Today when writing an OpInfo the operator's supported dtypes must be explicitly specified, and if those dtypes vary across device types or on different versions of CUDA those variants must be specified, too. These dtype specifications can be simple or complicated, here's part of the addmm OpInfo as a complicated example:
OpInfo('addmm',
  ...
  dtypes=floating_and_complex_types_and(torch.float16),
  dtypesIfCPU=all_types_and_complex_and(torch.float16, torch.bfloat16),
  dtypesIfROCM=floating_and_complex_types_and(torch.float16, torch.bfloat16),
  dtypesIfCUDA=floating_and_complex_types_and(torch.float16, *[torch.bfloat16] if CUDA11OrLater else []),

Understanding which dtypes to specify can be tricky, sometimes requiring trial and error if the operation is composite, and if a user doesn't have access to a CUDA device then this requires trial and error with the PyTorch CI to set dtypes properly. Worse, setting dtypes may still require trial and error with PyTorch CI because different platforms may support different dtypes (like in the addmm case above).
A partial solution to this is to provide a tool that indicates which dtypes an operator supports, but that doesn't address the challenge of users who lack a CUDA device or when platform differences cause dtype differences.
One idea, then, is to let OpInfos specify that their dtypes should be programmatically determined by the test suite. This would change the above addmm OpInfo into something like:
OpInfo('addmm',
  ...
  dtypes=floating_and_complex_types_and(torch.float16, torch.bfloat16),
  dtypesIfCUDA=_PROGRAMMATIC,

And when the OpInfo was created it would run a test to determine the appropriate CUDA dtypes (which would be inherited by ROCm, too).
There are pros and cons to this change. Pros:

it lets users without CUDA devices write OpInfos without going back and forth with CI
it simplifies writing OpInfos where an operator's dtypes vary on different platforms

Cons:

OpInfos using this pattern would no longer specify the dtypes an operator supports
OpInfos using this pattern could have their supported dtypes change and there would be no test signal when that occurred

Overall I think the improved accessibility overweighs the cons, and we can always replace _PROGRAMMATIC or _DYNAMIC or whatever we call it with an actual list of dtypes later if we prefer it.
Please share your thoughts below!
cc @mruberry @VitalyFedyunin @walterddr @eellison @Krovatkin @ngimel @kshitij12345 @krshrimali @pmeier @anjali411 @heitorschueroff @jbschlosser @albanD

🐛 Bug: Cannot deterministically load frozen model (saved after torch.jit.freeze)
When trying to export models to a mobile device, I noticed that torch.jit.freeze produces unexpected results.
Based on the existing documentation, I expected that:

frozen modules can be saved and loaded without changing their internal structure
running torch.jit.freeze on an already frozen module doesn't change its graph

Neither of which is the case in my scenario, I included the minimal snippet of code to reproduce my issues below.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
import torch
import torchvision.transforms.functional as F

# 0. load model
model = torch.hub.load("pytorch/vision:v0.9.0", "mobilenet_v2", pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# 1. trace
model1 = torch.jit.trace(model, example_inputs=[
    F.normalize(
        torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224),
        mean=torch.tensor([0.485, 0.456, 0.406]),
        std=torch.tensor([0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
    )
])
print(model1.graph)

# 2. freeze
model1 = model1.eval()  # otherwise, model1.training is undefined and torch.jit.freeze fails
model2 = torch.jit.freeze(model1)
print(model2.graph)  # inlined constants produce longer flattened graph, as expected

# 3. save both models
model1.save("model1.pt")
model2.save("model2.pt")

# 4. load the model that was not frozen - works as expected
model1_loaded = torch.jit.load("model1.pt")
print(model1_loaded.graph)  # equal to model1.graph, as expected

# 5. load the frozen model

To Reproduce

2.Training on GPU, there is no abnormality during training
3.Tested on the CPU, it is found that the speed of the model in the case of 0.001 and 0.01 is 5~6 times slower than 0.0001 in the case of eval()
Because the model code is not convenient to put up, I imitated    #51539  and wrote a test code
import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.optim import Adam, SGD, AdamW, Adadelta


class MLPQFunction(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.q = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(obs_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, 1)
        )

    def forward(self, obs, act):
        return self.q(obs)


def sac(device, lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.0):
    q_function = MLPQFunction(20, 256)
    q_function.to(device)
    q_optimizer = Adam(q_function.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    for j in range(100000000):
        q_function.train()
        q_optimizer.zero_grad()
        o, a = torch.rand(256, 20, device=device), torch.rand(256, 20, device=device)
        q = q_function(o, a)
        backup = torch.rand(256, device=device)
        loss_q = ((q - backup) ** 2).mean()
        loss_q.backward()
        q_optimizer.step()
        if j % 5000 == 0:
            q_function.eval()
            o, a = torch.rand(256, 20, device=device), torch.rand(256, 20, device=device)
            start = time.time()
            q = q_function(o, a)
            print(f'Time cost: %.5fs' % (time.time() - start))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    import argparse

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--weight-decay', type=float, default=0.001)
    parser.add_argument('--cuda', action='store_true', default=False)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    use_cuda = args.cuda and torch.cuda.is_available()
    device = torch.device("cpu")
    if not use_cuda:
        torch.set_num_threads(2)

import torch
import torch.fx

class Foo(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        with torch.profiler.record_function('my_op'):
            return torch.relu(x)

traced = torch.fx.symbolic_trace(Foo())
print(traced.code)
"""
def forward(self, x):
    relu = torch.relu(x);  x = None
    return relu
"""

A user may want their record_function ranges to be preserved in the FX-traced code. The initial conception of this was to support context managers, however I don't think it's worth it to do that since the value prop of FX is to have a flat DAG of operations without confusing nested scopes. Instead, we could record the underlying torch.ops.profiler._record_function_enter and torch.ops.profiler._record_function_exit calls in the graph. This would preserve the behavior, however it would not invoke _record_function_exit on propagating an exception. This is probably a fine trade-off
cc @ezyang @SherlockNoMad

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
Make remote module instantiation async
Motivation
Currently creating a RemoteModule is not async. meaning that by calling RemoteModule constructor, the caller has to wait until the module instantiated on the remote worker/device before it can continue. That's adds up to many hours if the user has hundreds of remote modules to be created (e.g. a GPT3 model to be created on 100 gpus).
This all can be async since RemoteModule stores an RRef to the module in remote worker.

🐛 Bug
We're hitting a QNNPACK race condition, when executing quantized convolutions concurrently in more than 1 thread.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Run the following script
import random
import threading

import torch

torch.set_grad_enabled(False)
torch.backends.quantized.engine = "qnnpack"


def _make_quant_layer():
    layer = torch.nn.intrinsic.ConvReLU2d(
        torch.nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), torch.nn.ReLU()
    )
    layer.qconfig = torch.quantization.default_per_channel_qconfig
    fake_model = torch.nn.Sequential(layer)
    torch.quantization.prepare(fake_model, inplace=True)
    fake_model(torch.zeros(1, 64, 1, 1))
    layer = torch.nn.intrinsic.quantized.ConvReLU2d.from_float(layer)
    return layer


class _RaceExperiment:
    def __init__(self, num_threads):
        self.module = torch.jit.script(
            torch.nn.Sequential(*[_make_quant_layer() for _ in range(50)])
        )
        self.module.eval()

        self.enter_barrier = threading.Barrier(num_threads)
        self.exit_barrier = threading.Barrier(num_threads)
        self.num_threads = num_threads

    def thread_run(self):
        data = torch.zeros((1, 64, 50, random.choice([50, 100, 200, 400])))
        data = torch.quantize_per_tensor(data, 1.0, 0, dtype=torch.quint8)
        self.enter_barrier.wait()
        self.module(data)
        self.exit_barrier.wait()
        self.module(data)

    def run_experiment(self):
        threads = [
            threading.Thread(target=self.thread_run) for _ in range(self.num_threads)
        ]
        for t in threads:
            t.start()
        for t in threads:
            t.join()
        print("done")


_RaceExperiment(1).run_experiment()

for _ in range(10):
    _RaceExperiment(3).run_experiment()

the following message:

         for module in self:
             input = module(input)
                     ~~~~~~ <--- HERE
         return input

             input = F.pad(input, _reversed_padding_repeated_twice,
                           mode=self.padding_mode)
         return torch.ops.quantized.conv2d_relu(
                ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ <--- HERE

 RuntimeError: pack_w != nullptr INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp":678, please report a bug to PyTorch. Packed Weights are NULL



Expected behavior
The script should finish without any issues. This can be achieved either by using the FBGEMM
backend or setting num_threads = 1 in _RaceExperiment.
Environment
Please copy and paste the output from our
environment collection script
(or fill out the checklist below manually).

Additional context
We've ran into this issue on one of our client's machines, so the bug is not theoretical. The actual
issue we observed there was the error message:
RuntimeError: pack_w != nullptr INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp":678, please report a bug to PyTorch. Packed Weights are NULL

(this is adapted to 1.8.1 since we run on 1.7.1, but I'm able to reproduce with the above script on
1.8.1)
Unfortunately we can't access AVX2 on that machine, so we cannot use FBGEMM.
My hypothesis of the cause of the race condition is the following:

Before the first execution of the convolution, PackedConvWeightsQnnp::w is nullptr and
PackedConvWeightsQnnp::input_scale doesn't contain a value (as outlined in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v1.8.1/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qconv_prepack.cpp#L254-L257)
One of the threads starts executing enters https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v1.8.1/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp#L604
and stores a value in PackedConvWeightsQnnp::input_scale, but hasn't yet assigned
PackedConvWeightsQnnp::w
Another thread sees that value of PackedConvWeightsQnnp::input_scale, skips the branch on https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v1.8.1/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp#L604,
reaches https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v1.8.1/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp#L678 and exits
with the error we see above.

At the moment the eigenvalues are returned in linalg.eigh in ascending order, while the singular values in linalg.svd are returned in descending order.
This dissonance is annoying but it goes in line with Numpy. Even then, we should at least give the user a nice interface to ask for the order they want the spectral values in. The name of the flag is in line with that present in torch.sort.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
At 
  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/cpu/vec256/vec256_base.h
    
    
         Line 706
      in
      43f6deb
    
  
  
    

        
          
           const intmax_t *a_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const intmax_t*>((const T*) a); 
        
    
  

 an invalid reinterpret_cast is made: reinterpret_cast<const intmax_t*>((const T*) a);
This casts a pointer to T (e.g. int32_t) to an unrelated type which is according to the C++ standard undefined behavior.
In PyTorch 1.7.1 this codepath was used on e.g. POWER archs (no AVX) and did in fact lead to bugs when handling tensors of size of at least 16.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

python -c 'import torch; print(torch.ones(16, dtype=torch.int32, device="cpu") & torch.ones(16, dtype=torch.int32, device="cpu"))'

Yields e.g.
tensor([18939904,     8192,        0,        0,        0,        0,        0,
               0, 18939904,     8192,        0,        0,        0,        0,
               0,        0], dtype=torch.int32)

Expected behavior
Output is correct (all 1s)
Environment
PyTorch 1.7.1 with GCC 10.2.0 on POWER9 (no CUDA)
Additional context
The correct way here would be using e.g. memcpy or something like the new std::bit_cast
This is optimized just the same but does not invoke undefined behavior and hence is correct even on POWER. See https://godbolt.org/z/K9foc8Y11 for a comparison of optimization
I'd also suggest to check the remaining code base for similar issues. Bugs like this are very hard to diagnose as even unrelated changes could trigger or disable them and as seen in this case upgrading the compiler can make those issues into real bugs due to new or more aggressive optimizations
Edit: One could also use the cast implementation for Vec256: https://godbolt.org/z/n4554v9xb
cc @VitalyFedyunin
